title: Reciprocity priority for registered organ donors
short_description: A national deceased-donor allocation authority must decide whether prior organ-donor registration should provide no priority, a bounded bonus, or stronger reciprocal priority after core clinical criteria are applied.
decision_question: Should prior registration as an organ donor provide additional allocation priority if that person later needs a transplant?
jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral allocation-policy case informed by current U.S. allocation practice and Israel's statutory donor-card priority system.

stipulations.statement: Medical compatibility, minimum transplant eligibility and core urgency criteria are applied before any donor-registration reciprocity factor.
stipulations.rationale: The benchmark tests whether registration should add priority rather than replace clinical suitability.

stipulations.statement: Any credited donor registration occurred before the candidate became seriously ill or knew of the present transplant need.
stipulations.rationale: Reciprocity should represent prior willingness to contribute rather than strategic registration after becoming a likely recipient.

stipulations.statement: The allocation system can exempt candidates who lacked a fair opportunity to register because of age, disability, access barriers or comparable circumstances.
stipulations.rationale: This keeps the reciprocity dispute from collapsing into punishment for inability to register.

stipulations.statement: The policy concerns prior deceased-donor registration, not actual prior living organ donation.
stipulations.rationale: Actual living donors often receive separate allocation recognition and are a different reciprocity case.

position_families: stronger reciprocal priority after basic clinical criteria

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored organ-allocation case grounded in public preference studies, current U.S. allocation practice and Israel's donor-card priority policy. It fixes prior registration, clinical criteria and fair-opportunity exemptions so the represented dispute is the additional weight, if any, assigned to reciprocal donor registration.

public.text: Do not add donor-registration status to allocation priority; rank clinically eligible candidates by medical and ordinary fairness criteria without rewarding prior registration.

provenance.summary: Adapted from public allocation-preference evidence in which donor-registration status received low or no preferred weight relative to prognosis, waiting time and other medical/fairness criteria.

sources.citation: Elalouf A, Pliskin JS, Kogut T. Attitudes, knowledge, and preferences of the Israeli public regarding the allocation of donor organs for transplantation. Isr J Health Policy Res. 2020;9(1):25. Telephone survey of 604 adults; donor-registration status ranked the least significant allocation criterion by 43%, against maximum medical benefit (51.3%) and waiting time (21%). PMID 32366325.
Oedingen C, Bartling T, Schrem H, et al. Public preferences for the allocation of donor organs for transplantation: a discrete choice experiment. Soc Sci Med. 2021;287:114360. PMID 34507218.

public.text: Give candidates who registered as organ donors before becoming seriously ill a modest allocation bonus or tie-break after core clinical criteria, with exemptions for people who lacked a fair opportunity to register.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from studies documenting meaningful public support for reciprocity priority and significant positive weight for registered-donor status. The modest bonus and fair-opportunity exemptions are Bench-authored policy completion that keeps reciprocity subordinate to core clinical criteria.

expert.text: Allocate organs using the established medical utility, urgency, waiting-time, matching and justice factors without adding ordinary prior donor-card registration as a general allocation reward.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from current U.S. OPTN allocation architecture: HRSA's current allocation factors include medical and matching criteria and recognize prior living donation for kidney allocation, but ordinary donor-card registration is not a general priority factor. The no-registration-reward sentence makes that current architecture explicit for the benchmark.

expert.text: Give qualifying prior registered organ donors additional waiting-list priority over otherwise medically comparable candidates, while preserving the clinical conditions that govern transplant suitability and matching.

provenance.summary: Adapted directly from Israel's Adi donor-card priority policy, under which qualifying card holders receive transplant waiting-list priority over candidates with the same medical condition who did not sign a donor card.

sources.citation: Israel Organ Transplant Law, 2008, donor-card priority provisions, as described by the Israel Ministry of Health's 'Adi' donor-card materials, current through 2026. Registered donors and the families of actual donors receive credit points added to their waiting-list score, subject to a minimum registration period, while clinical suitability and matching continue to govern.

framework.text: Give donor registration no allocation weight because access to a lifesaving public resource should turn on clinical need, benefit and fair opportunity rather than judgments of civic deservingness.

provenance.summary: Derived from equal-need, anti-desert and public-resource justice reasoning. The executable no-reciprocity rule is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: HRSA/OPTN. Ethical Principles in the Allocation of Human Organs.

framework.text: Give prior registrants a modest bonus or tie-break when clinical claims are otherwise close because willingness to contribute to the donor pool can justify bounded reciprocity without dominating medical need or benefit.

provenance.summary: Derived from fair reciprocity: contribution willingness may merit limited recognition while preserving the priority of clinical claims and exemptions for inability to register. The executable bounded rule is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: Chandler JA, Burkell JA, Shemie SD. Priority in organ allocation to previously registered donors. PMID 23187060.

framework.text: Give prior registrants substantial additional priority once basic clinical criteria are met because a donation system depends on reciprocal willingness to give as well as receive and may legitimately discourage free-riding.

provenance.summary: Derived from reciprocal-cooperation and public-goods reasoning. The stronger priority rule is Bench-authored and remains downstream of basic clinical eligibility.

scenario: A national deceased-donor system depends on voluntary public participation and has persistent organ scarcity. The allocation authority is considering whether a person's prior willingness to join the donor pool should matter if that person later becomes a transplant candidate. For this benchmark, assume medical compatibility, minimum transplant eligibility and core urgency criteria are applied before any reciprocity factor, any credited donor registration occurred before the candidate became seriously ill or knew of the transplant need, the system can exempt candidates who lacked a fair opportunity to register because of age, disability or access barriers, and the policy concerns deceased-donor registration rather than actual prior living donation. The authority must choose whether registration carries no allocation weight, a modest bonus or tie-break among otherwise close candidates, or stronger reciprocal priority after basic clinical criteria are satisfied.
